title: Fingering-weight lace stole
subtitle: A wide lace panel in fingering-weight yarn, worked flat from end to end.
excerpt: A straight stole knitted flat in a ten-row Shetland-inspired lace repeat on 3.75 mm needles with fingering-weight wool, finishing at 55 cm wide by 180 cm long after blocking. The wide format uses three panels of the same twelve-stitch lace repeat separated by narrow purl columns, and the whole piece is pinned out to its full dimensions to open the lace after knitting.
sourceNotes: Shetland lace stole patterns appear in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive. The tradition of wide lace stoles in Shetland two-ply is documented in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), citations only. The wave-and-fan lace structure draws on the Horseshoe lace described in multiple Victorian needlework manuals.

glossaryTerms.definition: Wrapping the working yarn over the right needle between stitches to create a new stitch and an eyelet. UK: yfwd (between knit stitches) or yrn (between purl stitches); US: yo.
Slip, slip, knit: slip two stitches knitwise, then knit them together through the back loops. Left-leaning decrease.
Knit two stitches together as one. Right-leaning decrease.
Soaking the finished piece in cool water, pressing out excess water, and pinning to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat while it dries. Essential for opening any lace to its full shape.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers. Produces one row of knitting as it sets up.
A traditional Shetland-derived lace motif in which yarn-overs and decreases form a horseshoe or arch shape across a twelve-stitch repeat. A staple of Victorian and Edwardian stole patterns.

content.text: This is a stole knitted flat from one short end to the other in a ten-row
horseshoe lace

repeat, finishing at 55 cm wide and 180 cm long after blocking. Three twelve-stitch lace panels run the full length, separated by single purl columns that frame each panel cleanly. The piece draws on the Shetland lace tradition, which uses the same family of
yarn-overs
and
SSK
and
k2tog
decreases to produce wave-and-arch motifs across wide panels.

Flat construction was chosen because a stole this wide, at 116 stitches, is most comfortable to work back and forth on a long circular needle with the fabric resting on the cord. The stole needs approximately 750 m (around 200 g) of fingering-weight two-ply or lace-weight yarn. Before blocking the fabric looks dense and slightly ruffled; after wet blocking and pinning to the full 55 x 180 cm it opens into its characteristic open-mesh arch pattern. The finished stole drapes over both shoulders and can also be wrapped and pinned as a large neck scarf.
What you need

items.name: Fingering-weight wool or wool-silk yarn, two-ply preferred
items.substitutions: Any fingering-weight yarn with elasticity. Wool or a wool-silk blend pins open and holds the lace shape well. Superwash wool loses some elasticity and the arches may relax more after blocking.

items.name: 3.75 mm circular needle, 80 cm or longer (UK 9 / US 5)
items.substitutions: A long circular is necessary for the stitch count; the work is still knitted flat.

items.name: Stitch markers
items.qty: 4 (to mark the purl columns between panels)

items.name: Blocking mat, minimum 55 x 180 cm, and rust-proof pins
items.substitutions: Several interlocking mats placed end to end. Allow 60 cm of mat width to pin the edges comfortably.

content.text: Gauge

24 sts x 32 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked. In horseshoe lace pattern, the gauge is approximately 20 sts per 10 cm because the lace fans the fabric slightly wider. Swatch a full 12-stitch repeat, block the swatch, and measure dry. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by approximately 2.75 cm at this stitch count (116 sts): at 21 sts per 10 cm the stole finishes around 52 cm wide; at 19 sts per 10 cm it finishes around 58 cm wide. Row gauge drift across the full 504 rows changes the finished length by up to 15 cm.
Stitches used
K (knit): right needle from left to right through front of stitch, wrap yarn counterclockwise, draw loop through.
P (purl): right needle from right to left through front of stitch with yarn in front, wrap yarn, draw loop through to back.
YO (yarn over, UK: yfwd): bring yarn to front between needles and over the right needle tip before the next knit stitch.
SSK: slip two stitches knitwise one at a time, return to left needle in new orientation, knit through the back loops together. Left-leaning decrease.
K2tog: knit two stitches together through the front loops. Right-leaning decrease.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 116 stitches on the needle. The stitch count is: 3 garter border + 3 panels of 12 sts (36 sts) + 2 purl column separators (2 sts) + additional panel fill to 110 centre sts + 3 garter border, totalling 116 sts. Before beginning, calculate the tail length: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 3.75 mm needles (circumference approximately 11.8 mm) and 116 stitches: (11.8 x 116) / 10 + 15 = 136.9 + 15 = about 152 cm. Leave a tail of at least 152 cm before the slip knot; a length of roughly 1.5 m is easier to manage if you wind it loosely around your thumb.

Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 116 stitches on the needle. Place markers after stitch 3, after stitch 38 (marking the first purl column), after stitch 77 (marking the second purl column), and before the last 3 stitches.
Body

The garter border is 3 stitches knitted on every row. Between borders, a RS row runs: K3 border, Panel 1 (12-st horseshoe x 3), slip marker, P1 column, slip marker, Panel 2 (12-st horseshoe x 3), slip marker, P1 column, slip marker, Panel 3 (12-st horseshoe x 3), K3 border.
Row 1 (RS): K3, [K1, YO, K4, SSK, K2tog, K4, YO] 3 times in each panel across markers, K3. Maintain purl column stitches at each separator. (116 sts)
Row 2 (WS): K3, P across all stitches to last 3 (purl the purl columns, purl the panel stitches), K3. (116 sts)

Continue the 10-row chart, shifting the YO placement by one stitch each RS row as charted, until the stole measures 180 cm from the cast-on edge. At the halfway point (approximately row 252, around 90 cm), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 252 you should have 116 stitches on the needle.
Bind off

Work a suspended bind-off on a right-side row: K2, *slip both stitches back to the left needle, K2tog, K1; repeat from * to the end. For a stole at 116 stitches, a tight bind-off can lose 3 to 5 cm of finished length at the bound-off end. If the bound-off edge still feels tight after the first 10 stitches, switch to a needle two sizes larger for the remainder of the bind-off row.
Common faults

Stitch count rising panel by panel. Each horseshoe repeat must end with the same stitch count it began with: two yarn-overs and two decreases in every right-side row. A rising count usually means a missed K2tog or SSK. Check by row not just at major checkpoints.

One panel shifted against the others. This happens when the markers drift out of position or are moved accidentally. Recount stitches between each marker at the end of any row where something feels off.
Stole too narrow after blocking. The full width depends on firm, generous pinning at 55 cm. Pin every 2 to 3 cm along both long edges. A sparse-pinned stole can dry 4 to 6 cm narrower than intended.

Stocking-stitch curling at the garter border join. If the 3-stitch garter border is not enough to hold the edge flat on a very light yarn, add one extra garter stitch on each side. The body stitch count stays the same; only the border grows.
Finishing
Weave in both tails along the back of the garter border, changing direction once. For a stole with only two ends the weaving is fast.
Wet blocking

is non-negotiable for a lace stole. Soak in cool water for 30 minutes, gently press out the water without wringing, roll in a clean dry towel to remove excess moisture, and then lay flat on the blocking mat. Pin the short cast-on end square first, then walk the long edges out to 55 cm, pinning every 3 cm, then stretch and pin the bound-off short end to the full 180 cm. Leave flat and undisturbed until completely dry, which may take 24 hours for a wool stole this wide.
Care

Handwash in cool water with a small amount of wool wash, supporting the full wet weight. Roll in a towel to remove excess water, then pin flat to the stated dimensions and leave to dry completely. The stole does not need re-pinning after every wash but should be laid fully flat rather than draped over a rail.
What to try next

From a lace stole the natural next project is a triangular lace shawl, which uses increases at the centre spine or edges to build the triangular shape from a small cast-on. The same horseshoe repeat can be used across the body of a shawl exactly as it runs across this stole.
